strengths: The paper addresses an important efficiency bottleneck in multimodal models. Reducing 576 visual tokens to approximately 40 while retaining substantial task performance is potentially valuable, even with some accuracy loss.
Evaluation covers six benchmarks and both 7B and 13B LLaVA-1.5 models. After fine-tuning, ScienceQA and POPE performance remains close to, or slightly exceeds, the corresponding baseline.

The ablations provide useful evidence: training-free PruMerge achieves 54.00 TextVQA versus 47.96 for the best reported spatial sampler (Table 3), and adding token supplementation improves MME from 1221.6 to 1350.3 (Table 4).

The high-level pipeline is understandable, and the manuscript cites its underlying models, datasets, and prior pruning and merging methods. It also explicitly acknowledges lossy compression and limited validation scope.
weaknesses: The comparisons do not establish the added value of the proposed adaptive selection and merging combination. Table 3 primarily compares against retaining the first 40 tokens and regular spatial grids. Missing controls include fixed-budget attention ranking with the same merging procedure and established token-merging approaches at comparable budgets. An accuracy-versus-token-budget curve would help establish whether PruMerge offers a superior tradeoff. Comparisons with unrelated multimodal architectures in Table 1 do not resolve this concern.

Practical efficiency remains insufficiently validated. Section 4.2 and Table 2 provide roofline estimates for a particular prefill scenario, rather than measured latency, throughput, or peak memory. They do not establish end-to-end savings after visual encoding, selection and clustering overhead, variable-length batching, and autoregressive decoding. The manuscript appropriately labels these estimates as theoretical, but measured results are important for its central efficiency contribution.

The characterization of performance degradation as marginal is too strong. In Table 1, VQAv2 drops from 78.5 to 72.0 for 7B and from 80.0 to 72.8 for 13B; 7B MME drops from 1510.7 to 1350.3. Without fine-tuning, POPE falls from 85.9 to 76.2 (Table 5). These losses may be acceptable for substantial compression, but they qualify claims of preserving reasoning capabilities and broadly comparable performance.

Important implementation details are ambiguous. Algorithm 1 excludes the selected center from its neighbor candidates and replaces it with an unnormalized weighted sum, whereas the narrative describes supplementation and weighted averaging. The neighbor count k, attention-head aggregation, and handling of overlapping clusters are unspecified. LoRA rank, learning rate, and other training settings are also absent. These issues prevent confident reproduction; they do not by themselves prove that the implementation is incorrect.

The adaptive mechanism is weakly validated. A sparse attention plot and a few visualizations do not establish that IQR outlier counts reliably track image complexity or identify an optimal token budget. No quantitative token-count distribution, threshold sensitivity, or comparison against a fixed count with matched average computation is supplied. Experiments also remain within one model family at 336-pixel resolution, leaving the motivating high-resolution and video applications untested.
